en: *Saṃvarodaya-tantra*: "The Chapter on the Exposition of Reality" (*Tattva-nirdeśa-paṭala*);
Sanskrit Text and Japanese Translation, edited and translated by Shinichi Tsuda.
*Bukkyōgaku* (Journal of Buddhist Studies), Vol. 1, July 1976, pp. 27–45. ^30
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the cultivation of the reality of things as they truly are:
how cultivation is itself the nature of existence, yet is non-existence and free from conceptual proliferation.
Action consists of self-awareness, and even meditative cultivation is devoid of a cultivator;
being free from unity and plurality, it arises as nothing other than the momentary.
This knowledge, self-cognizable and having as its object that which transcends the meaning of words, arises in a wondrous form, consisting of the very essence of the omniscient one’s knowledge. (3)

Equal to the intrinsic nature of all phenomena; light yet difficult to fathom; devoid of causes; self-manifesting; luminous by nature; beyond the scope of investigation; free from dispute; peaceful; certain; unprovoked; inexpressible; indefinable; abiding as the intrinsic nature of all phenomena; having the form of emptiness; devoid of qualities such as sound and the rest. || 4 ||
This source of the arising of the Buddha’s bliss, upon which the world is established, has not been revealed by me; it is some incomparable state of awakening.
The peerless reality has been taught by the Victors;
it is graced by a clear and skillful consciousness that abandons the two aspects,
within the vault of the sky filled with the supreme essence and engraved with dense bliss.
Within the mind, in which all internal states have been accumulated by means of various shimmering forms, these three worlds appear as if they have gone to dissolution;
this is called the innate nature, the single vow of all aspects. (6)
That very consciousness, characterized by all aspects, is the mandala;
all the channels are the dakinis, and all the sense bases are the mandala.
When all [phenomena] attain a single flavor, the form of Heruka manifests;
it is without appearance, not space, entirely without remainder, and without abode. || 8 ||
Because it is the intrinsic nature of all things, it is always present in all things;
therein, the true nature of entities is perceived by means of that very nature itself.
Formless bliss, this self-existent one, arises;
likewise, through the state of non-mind, the mind becomes the awakener of the single universe.
Wherein it shines by itself, free from the distinction between existence and non-existence,
that majesty of awakening consists of intense bliss and pervades the interior of space.

Spreading out in various forms yet shimmering like the circle of a mirror due to its purity, that innate bliss (*sahajānanda*), which is generally the abode of all happiness, is designated as the fourth. (11)
Therein, neither wisdom nor means exists as the awakener of the true reality; all conceptualizations of yoginīs, the maṇḍala, and the three worlds [are that reality]. 12.
The sequence is: the Dharma, Enjoyment, Emanation, and Great Bliss;
the four wheels are equal in their nature as Great Bliss. (13)
Free from attachment, the yogi should always wander among all things;
unstained even in the midst of the mud of saṃsāra, he experiences the bliss of nirvāṇa.
Endowed with auspicious qualities, possessed of wisdom, and joined with vigor,
he then regards his teachers with devotion as equal to a Buddha;
having realized the Dharma of the Victors, he is perfectly serene in the teaching.
He becomes a worthy recipient here; one should show him favor.
Likewise, for yogins who possess a single consciousness of the three realms undifferentiated from form and the rest, there is also an uninterrupted bliss that is exceedingly powerful. (16)
As many as there are accumulations for enlightenment, so many are present here in their stainless form;
for the yogin, whose nature consists of wisdom and means, attains the unsurpassed fruit. (17)
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, the Exposition of Reality.
